section_title: Part I — The Union and its Territory (Overview)
section_desc: Part I (Articles 1-4) establishes India as a Union of States. Articles 1-4 deal with name and territory, admission of new States, formation of new States and alteration of areas. The word 'Union' was deliberately chosen over 'Federation' to indicate that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the States and the States have no right to secede from it (Constituent Assembly debates). India is an indestructible Union of destructible States.

section_title: Part II — Citizenship (Articles 5-11 Overview)
section_desc: Part II deals with citizenship at commencement of Constitution. Article 5: citizenship by domicile; Article 6: rights of citizenship of certain persons who migrated from Pakistan; Article 7: rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan; Article 8: rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India; Article 9: persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens; Article 10: continuance of rights of citizenship; Article 11: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship. The Citizenship Act, 1955 governs citizenship after commencement.

section_title: Article 13 — Laws inconsistent with fundamental rights (detailed)
section_desc: Article 13 is the guardian of Fundamental Rights. Sub-article (1): pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Part III are void to the extent of inconsistency. Sub-article (2): State shall not make laws abridging Fundamental Rights. Sub-article (3): 'law' includes ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom and usage. Sub-article (4): Constitutional amendments are not 'law' for this purpose (Shankari Prasad case 1951, later challenged in Golak Nath 1967, resolved in Kesavananda Bharati 1973 — basic structure doctrine).

section_title: Article 16(4) — Reservations in public employment
section_desc: Article 16(4) empowers the State to make provision for reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. Article 16(4A): reservation in promotion for SCs and STs. Article 16(4B): carry forward of unfilled reserved vacancies. The ceiling of 50% on total reservations was set in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal case, 1992).

section_title: Article 19 — Six freedoms of citizens (detailed)
section_desc: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms: (a) freedom of speech and expression; (b) right to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) right to form associations/unions/cooperative societies; (d) right to move freely throughout India; (e) right to reside and settle in any part of India; (g) right to practice any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. Article 19(2)-(6) permit reasonable restrictions by the State on grounds including sovereignty, public order, decency, morality. The right to privacy is part of Article 19(1)(a) (Puttaswamy case 2017).

section_title: Article 21 — Expanded scope by Supreme Court
section_desc: Article 21 has been expansively interpreted: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) — procedure must be fair, just and reasonable; Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) — right to live with dignity; Olga Tellis (1985) — right to livelihood; Vincent Panikurlangara (1987) — right to health; Mohini Jain (1992) — right to education; Unni Krishnan (1993) — free and compulsory education upto 14 years; MC Mehta (1991) — right to pollution-free environment; NALSA v. Union of India (2014) — rights of transgender persons; Puttaswamy (2017) — right to privacy as fundamental right.

section_title: Article 22 — Safeguards against arrest (detailed)
section_desc: Article 22 provides: (1) right to be informed of grounds of arrest; (2) right to consult and be defended by lawyer of choice; (3) right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours of arrest; (4) right not to be detained beyond 24 hours without magistrate's authority (police can detain max 24 hours). Article 22(4)-(7) deal with Preventive Detention: maximum initial detention 3 months; Advisory Board must confirm beyond 3 months; detainee must be informed of grounds; right to make representation. Article 22 does not apply to enemy alien or person detained under preventive detention law.

section_title: Article 29 — Protection of interests of minorities
section_desc: Article 29(1): Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. Article 29(2): No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.

section_title: Article 31A — Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates
section_desc: Article 31A saves certain laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19: laws providing for acquisition by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights; laws relating to management of properties pending acquisition; laws relating to amalgamation of corporations; laws relating to extinguishment of rights of directors or managing agents; laws relating to extinguishment of mining leases. Added by 1st Constitutional Amendment 1951 to protect land reforms.

section_title: Article 31B — Validation of certain Acts and Regulations (Ninth Schedule)
section_desc: Without prejudice to the generality of Article 31A, none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule nor any of the provisions thereof shall be deemed to be void on the ground that such Act, regulation or provision is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by, any provisions of Part III. The Ninth Schedule was added by 1st Amendment 1951. SC in IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws added to Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati) can be challenged if they damage the basic structure.

section_title: Article 31C — Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
section_desc: Notwithstanding anything contained in Article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV (DPSP) shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by Article 14, 19, or 31. Added by 25th Amendment 1971. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the words 'any of the principles' were struck down — only laws implementing DPSP Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are protected.

section_title: Article 40 — Organisation of village panchayats
section_desc: The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment 1992 (Articles 243-243O) gave constitutional status to panchayats, mandating reservation for SCs, STs and women (not less than one-third), elections every five years, and establishment of State Finance Commissions and State Election Commissions.

section_title: Article 51 — Promotion of international peace and security
section_desc: The State shall endeavour to: promote international peace and security; maintain just and honourable relations between nations; foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration. This DPSP guides India's foreign policy. International treaties ratified by India can be implemented by Parliament under Article 253.

section_title: Article 51A — Fundamental Duties (detailed)
section_desc: Article 51A was added by 42nd Amendment 1976 (originally 10 duties). The 86th Amendment 2002 added duty (k): who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of 6 and 14 years. The eleven duties include: abide by Constitution; cherish noble ideals of freedom struggle; uphold sovereignty, unity, integrity; defend country; promote harmony; preserve cultural heritage; protect environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property; strive for excellence; provide education to children. Fundamental duties are not enforceable by court but can guide interpretation of laws.

section_title: Article 53 — Executive power of the Union
section_desc: The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution. The supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President. The exercise thereof shall be regulated by law. The President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74) — the President is a constitutional head, not an executive president.

section_title: Article 74 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
section_desc: There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice. Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration. The advice of the Council of Ministers shall not be enquired into by any court.

section_title: Article 76 — Attorney General for India
section_desc: The President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court to be Attorney General for India. It shall be the duty of the Attorney General to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the President, and to discharge the functions conferred on him by or under this Constitution. The Attorney General shall have the right of audience in all courts in India.

section_title: Article 79 — Constitution of Parliament
section_desc: There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People. The Council of States (Rajya Sabha) is the upper house — 238 elected/nominated representatives of States plus 12 nominated by President. The House of the People (Lok Sabha) — maximum 552 members (530 from States, 20 from Union Territories, 2 nominated Anglo-Indians — abolished by 104th Amendment 2019).

section_title: Article 100 — Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
section_desc: Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting. The Speaker or Chairman, as the case may be, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes. A quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House.

section_title: Article 105 — Powers, privileges and immunities of Parliament and its members
section_desc: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament. No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof. No person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings.

section_title: Article 108 — Joint sitting of both Houses
section_desc: In certain cases, the President may summon the Houses to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose of deliberating and voting on: a Bill which has been passed by one House and rejected by the other; a Bill in respect of which the other House has not passed it within the period of six months from the date of its receipt by that House; or a Bill in respect of which the other House has passed it with amendments to which the first House does not agree.

section_title: Article 110 — Definition of Money Bills
section_desc: A Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; the regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India; the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund; the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India.

section_title: Article 112 — Annual Financial Statement (Budget)
section_desc: The President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year, referred to in this Part as the Annual Financial Statement. The statement shall show the receipts and expenditure of the Government under the three parts — Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account. All expenditure is classified as Charged or Voted.

section_title: Article 118 — Rules of procedure
section_desc: Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, its procedure and the conduct of its business. Until rules are made by a House, the rules of procedure and standing orders in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution with respect to the Legislature of the Dominion of India shall apply to that House with such modifications as the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be, may make.

section_title: Article 123 — Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
section_desc: If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require. An Ordinance promulgated shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament. It ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament or if both Houses disapprove it.

section_title: Article 148 — Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
section_desc: There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The CAG shall not be removed from office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament. The CAG shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as may be prescribed by law made by Parliament.

section_title: Article 153 — Governors of States
section_desc: There shall be a Governor for each State. Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent the appointment of the same person as Governor for two or more States. The Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. The Governor is the constitutional head of the State as the President is of the Union.

section_title: Article 163 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor
section_desc: There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion. If any question arises whether any matter is or is not a matter as respects which the Governor is by or under this Constitution required to act in his discretion, the decision of the Governor in his discretion shall be final.

section_title: Article 200 — Assent to Bills by Governor
section_desc: When a Bill has been passed by the Legislative Assembly of a State or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, has been passed by both Houses of the Legislature of the State, it shall be presented to the Governor and the Governor shall declare either that he assents to the Bill, or that he withholds assent therefrom, or that he reserves the Bill for the consideration of the President.

section_title: Article 212 — Courts not to inquire into proceedings of the Legislature
section_desc: The validity of any proceedings in the Legislature of a State shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure. No officer or member of the Legislature of a State in whom powers are vested by or under this Constitution for regulating procedure or the conduct of business, or for maintaining order, in the Legislature shall be subject to the jurisdiction of any court in respect of the exercise by him of those powers.

section_title: Article 239AA — Special provisions with respect to Delhi
section_desc: Delhi shall be known as the National Capital Territory of Delhi. There shall be a Legislative Assembly for the National Capital Territory. The Legislative Assembly shall have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the NCT with respect to any of the matters in the State List or Concurrent List in so far as any such matter is applicable to Union Territories except matters with respect to Entries 1, 2 and 18 of the State List and Entries 64, 65 and 66 of that List in so far as they relate to the said Entries 1, 2 and 18.

section_title: Article 245 — Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
section_desc: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State. No law made by Parliament shall be deemed to be invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation.
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States

section_title: Article 246 — Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by Legislatures of States
section_desc: Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I (Union List — 97 subjects). The Legislature of any State has power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II (State List — 66 subjects). Parliament and Legislature of each State have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III (Concurrent List — 47 subjects). In case of conflict between Parliament and State law on a Concurrent List subject, Parliamentary law prevails (Article 254).
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States
keywords: List I List II List III

section_title: Article 248 — Residuary powers of legislation
section_desc: Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List. Such power shall include the power of making any law imposing a tax not mentioned in either of those Lists. The residuary power is vested in Parliament — this is different from federations like Canada and Australia where residuary power may be with provinces.
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States

section_title: Article 254 — Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by Legislatures of States
section_desc: If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States

section_title: Article 256 — Obligation of States and the Union
section_desc: The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose. Failure to comply with Union directions can lead to President's Rule (Article 356).
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States

section_title: Article 262 — Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys
section_desc: Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley. Parliament may also provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was enacted under this Article.
chapter_title: Relations between the Union and the States

section_title: Article 265 — Taxes not to be imposed save by authority of law
section_desc: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. This Article is the constitutional basis for the rule 'no taxation without legislation'. Any tax levied without statutory authority is unconstitutional. The GST Constitutional Amendment (101st Amendment Act 2016) made fundamental changes to taxation — inserted Article 246A giving concurrent power to levy GST to both Parliament and States.

section_title: Articles 268-293 — Finance Relations (Overview)
section_desc: The Constitutional provisions on finance relations cover: Article 268 — duties levied by Union but collected by States; Article 269 — taxes levied and collected by Union but assigned to States; Article 270 — taxes levied and collected by Union and distributed between Union and States (Divisible Pool); Article 271 — surcharges; Article 272 — union excise duties sharing; Article 275 — grants-in-aid; Article 280 — Finance Commission (constituted every 5 years to recommend revenue sharing); Article 293 — borrowing by States.

section_title: Article 280 — Finance Commission
section_desc: The President shall, within two years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary, by order constitute a Finance Commission. The Finance Commission shall make recommendations as to: the distribution between the Union and the States of the net proceeds of taxes which are to be divided; the principles which should govern the grants-in-aid; the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State. The 15th Finance Commission recommendations covered 2021-26.

section_title: Article 300A — Right to property (post-44th Amendment)
section_desc: Article 300A was inserted by 44th Amendment 1978 which removed the fundamental right to property (original Articles 19(1)(f) and 31). It now provides: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' Property is now only a Constitutional right, not a fundamental right. The State can acquire property by law but must provide fair compensation. Writ under Article 32 does not lie for violation of Article 300A — only Article 226 (High Court) writ is available.

section_title: Article 315 — Public Service Commissions for the Union and for the States
section_desc: There shall be a Public Service Commission for the Union (UPSC) and a Public Service Commission for each State. Two or more States may agree to have one Joint Public Service Commission. The UPSC conducts examinations for appointments to the services of the Union. Members of UPSC are appointed by the President; members of State PSC are appointed by the Governor. A member of UPSC can be removed by the President on grounds of proved misbehaviour.
chapter_title: Services under the Union and the States

section_title: Article 311 — Dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of persons employed in civil capacities under the Union or a State
section_desc: No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India service or a civil service of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. No such person shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges.
chapter_title: Services under the Union and the States

section_title: Article 312 — All-India Services
section_desc: Notwithstanding anything in Chapter VI of Part VI or Part XI, if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest so to do, Parliament may by law provide for the creation of one or more all-India services (including an all-India judicial service) common to the Union and the States. The Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service are constitutionally recognised all-India services.
chapter_title: Services under the Union and the States

section_title: Article 340 — Appointment of a Commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes
section_desc: The President may by order appoint a Commission consisting of such persons as he thinks fit to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes within the territory of India and the difficulties under which they labour and to make recommendations as to the steps that should be taken by the Union or any State to remove such difficulties. The Mandal Commission was constituted under this Article.
chapter_title: Special Provisions relating to Certain Classes

section_title: Article 341 — Scheduled Castes
section_desc: The President may with respect to any State or Union Territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the castes, races or tribes or parts of or groups within castes, races or tribes which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Castes in relation to that State or Union Territory, as the case may be. Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Castes specified in a notification.
chapter_title: Special Provisions relating to Certain Classes

section_title: Article 342 — Scheduled Tribes
section_desc: The President may with respect to any State or Union Territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within tribes or tribal communities which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Tribes. Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Tribes. The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST reservations in Parliament and State Assemblies by 10 years to 2030.
chapter_title: Special Provisions relating to Certain Classes

section_title: Article 343 — Official language of the Union
section_desc: The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script. The form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals. English shall continue to be used for all official purposes for which it was being used before the commencement of this Constitution for a period of fifteen years. Parliament may by law provide for use of English after 15 years.

section_title: Article 348 — Language to be used in the Supreme Court and in the High Courts and for Acts, Bills, etc.
section_desc: All proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court shall be in the English language until Parliament by law otherwise provides. All Bills to be introduced or amendments thereto to be moved in either House of Parliament or in the House or Houses of the Legislature of a State, all Acts passed by Parliament or the Legislature of a State, and all orders, rules, regulations and bye-laws made under this Constitution shall be in the English language.

section_title: Article 360 — Provisions as to financial emergency
section_desc: If the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, he may by a Proclamation make a declaration to that effect. During Financial Emergency: the President may direct States to observe canons of financial propriety; salaries and allowances of all persons in service of India may be reduced; money bills passed by State Legislatures may be reserved for President's consideration. Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
section_desc: The Supreme Court by a 7:6 majority held: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution including fundamental rights under Article 368, BUT it cannot destroy the 'basic structure' of the Constitution. The basic structure doctrine includes: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, unity and integrity of India, sovereignty, judicial review, rule of law, free and fair elections, independence of judiciary. This remains the most important constitutional judgment in India.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
section_desc: The Supreme Court overruled AK Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) and held: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive but interdependent — the 'golden triangle'. Procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable (not just any procedure). The Court adopted a golden triangle interpretation: any law depriving a person of life or liberty must satisfy Article 14 (non-arbitrary), Article 19 (reasonable), and Article 21 (fair procedure). This judgment vastly expanded the scope of Article 21.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) — Mandal Case
section_desc: The Supreme Court (9-judge bench) upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4) but: (1) set a 50% ceiling on total reservations (creamy layer concept — well-off OBCs cannot claim reservation); (2) held no reservation in promotion (Parliament later added Article 16(4A) and 16(4B)); (3) held economic criterion alone cannot be the basis for reservation; (4) held backward classes must be identified by the State. This landmark judgment remains the cornerstone of reservation law in India.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
section_desc: The Supreme Court held: Article 356 (President's Rule) is subject to judicial review; the majority of a government should be tested on the floor of the House and not by the Governor's subjective satisfaction; secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution; the President's satisfaction for proclamation under Article 356 can be examined on the ground of mala fides and being founded on non-existent or irrelevant grounds. This judgment restricted the misuse of Article 356 by the Central Government.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Justice KS Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — Right to Privacy
section_desc: A 9-judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution. The right to privacy protects the dignity and autonomy of a person. Privacy includes: informational privacy, physical privacy, mental privacy, decisional autonomy. The judgment overruled the earlier judgments in MP Sharma (1958) and Kharak Singh (1963). It formed the constitutional basis for striking down Section 377 IPC (Navtej Singh Johar 2018) and triple talaq.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
section_desc: The Supreme Court unanimously struck down Section 377 IPC (unnatural offences) to the extent it criminalised consensual same-sex intercourse between adults. The Court held: sexual orientation is an inherent aspect of self-identity; criminalising consensual same-sex acts violates Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21; LGBTQ+ persons have full equality under the Constitution; the right to choose one's partner is part of Article 21. The judgment overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) which had restored Section 377.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
section_desc: The Supreme Court laid down guidelines to prevent sexual harassment of women at the workplace, filling a legislative vacuum. The Court drew from CEDAW and Constitutional provisions. The Vishaka guidelines: every employer must constitute a Complaints Committee; sexual harassment at workplace must be prohibited; awareness to be created among employees; annual report to government. These guidelines remained the law until replaced by the POSH Act 2013. The case arose from Bhanwari Devi gang rape.

section_title: Landmark Judgment — NALSA v. Union of India (2014)
section_desc: The Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as the 'third gender' and held: transgender persons have the right to self-identification of their gender; they are entitled to legal recognition as a 'third gender' other than male or female; reservation benefits for backward classes should be extended to them; Right to dignity and identity is guaranteed under Articles 14, 15, 16, 19 and 21; they should not be discriminated in employment, education, and healthcare. This judgment led to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.

section_title: 101st Constitutional Amendment — Goods and Services Tax
section_desc: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) by: inserting Article 246A — concurrent power of Parliament and States to levy GST; inserting Article 269A — levy of IGST on inter-State trade; creating the GST Council (Article 279A) with Finance Minister of India as Chairperson and Finance Ministers of all States as members; Parliament to provide for compensation to States for revenue loss for 5 years; abolishing Central Sales Tax. GST subsumed multiple central and state taxes.

section_title: 103rd Constitutional Amendment — 10% EWS Reservation
section_desc: The Constitution (103rd Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted: Article 15(6) — State may make special provision for economically weaker sections (EWS) up to 10% in addition to existing reservations, for admission to educational institutions including private unaided; Article 16(6) — State may provide up to 10% reservation in government jobs for EWS not covered by Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4). EWS means family income less than Rs 8 lakh per year. The Supreme Court upheld it in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) by 3:2 majority.

section_title: First Schedule — States and Union Territories
section_desc: The First Schedule lists all States and their territories and all Union Territories. Currently India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories. The Schedule is amended whenever new States are created or territories are reorganised. Key reorganisations: reorganisation of States on linguistic basis 1956; creation of Telangana from Andhra Pradesh 2014; Jammu & Kashmir reorganised into two UTs (J&K and Ladakh) by Reorganisation Act 2019; Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu merged into one UT 2020.

section_title: Seventh Schedule — Three Lists
section_desc: The Seventh Schedule contains three lists: List I (Union List) — 97 subjects on which only Parliament can legislate (defence, foreign affairs, currency, banking, railways, etc.); List II (State List) — 66 subjects on which only State Legislatures can legislate (police, public health, agriculture, land, etc.); List III (Concurrent List) — 47 subjects on which both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate (criminal law, marriage, bankruptcy, education, etc.). In case of conflict on Concurrent List, Parliamentary law prevails (Article 254).
keywords: List I List II List III

section_title: Ninth Schedule — Validation of Certain Acts and Regulations
section_desc: The Ninth Schedule was added by 1st Amendment 1951 to protect land reform laws from judicial review under fundamental rights. Laws included in the Ninth Schedule cannot be challenged in courts for violating Part III (Fundamental Rights). However, the Supreme Court in IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that laws included in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati date) can be examined for violation of basic structure of the Constitution. Currently the Schedule has 284 Acts.

section_title: Tenth Schedule — Anti-Defection Law
section_desc: The Tenth Schedule was added by 52nd Amendment 1985. It disqualifies members of Parliament and State Legislatures on grounds of defection: if a member voluntarily gives up membership of his political party; if a member votes or abstains from voting in the House contrary to directions issued by his political party without obtaining prior permission of such party. A member of a House shall not be disqualified if his original political party merges with another party and two-thirds of members agree to the merger.

section_title: Eleventh Schedule — Panchayati Raj (73rd Amendment)
section_desc: The Eleventh Schedule was added by 73rd Amendment 1992 and lists 29 subjects that may be entrusted to Panchayats: agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, social forestry, small scale industries, khadi, rural housing, drinking water, roads, rural electrification, poverty alleviation, education, markets, health, women and child development, social welfare, welfare of weaker sections, public distribution system, maintenance of community assets.

section_title: Twelfth Schedule — Municipalities (74th Amendment)
section_desc: The Twelfth Schedule was added by 74th Amendment 1992 and lists 18 functions that may be entrusted to Municipalities: urban planning, regulation of land-use, planning for economic and social development, roads and bridges, water supply, public health, fire services, urban forestry, protection of weaker sections, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, provision of urban amenities, promotion of cultural educational aesthetic aspects, burial grounds, vital statistics, public amenities.
